**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿His bearing and his weaning take thirty months.﴾

This noble verse, taken by itself, does not address the minimum period of pregnancy. However, when it is combined with some other verses, the minimum period of pregnancy becomes known. This noble verse in the surah of "al-Ahqaf" states that the period of pregnancy and weaning together is thirty months.

God Most High's words in "Luqman" are: ﴿and his weaning is in two years﴾. And His words in "al-Baqarah": ﴿Mothers suckle their children for two complete years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233] show that the period of weaning is two years, which equals twenty-four months. When you subtract them from thirty, six months remain, and so it is determined that this is the period of pregnancy, and it is the minimum. There is no disagreement about this among the scholars.

The indication of these verses that six months is the minimum period of pregnancy is what is known among the scholars of usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) as dalālat al-ishārah (indication by allusion).

We have explained the discussion of it in the chapters on Hajj, in the surah of "al-Hajj", in the discussion of the views of the scholars on the ruling on spending the night at Muzdalifah, and we pointed to this type of explanation in the introduction to this blessed book.

* *

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿Until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years﴾.

We have already presented the discussion of this verse in the surah of "al-An'am", in the discussion of God's words: ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾ [al-An'am: 152], and in the introduction to this blessed book.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 46, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both! Do you threaten me that I will be brought forth, when generations have passed before me?" And they both call upon Allah for help, "Woe to you! Believe, for indeed the promise of Allah is true." But he says, "This is nothing but the myths of the former peoples."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones upon whom the word has been justified.﴾

The verified view, if Allah wills, is that the relative pronoun in His saying "And the one who says" (wa-alladhi) means "those who" (alladhina), and that the verse is general, applying to every child who is disobedient to his parents and denies the Resurrection.

The Qur'anic evidence that alladhi means alladhina and that the intended sense is general is that alladhi in His saying "And the one who says to his parents" is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom the word has been justified﴾, and so on.

The reference, in His saying "Those are the ones upon whom the word has been justified", to the word alladhina in the plural form is clear evidence that the intended meaning of alladhi is generality, not singularity. The best thing by which the Qur'an is interpreted is the Qur'an itself.

By this Qur'anic evidence you know that the statement of those who said regarding this noble verse that it was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with both of them, is not correct, as 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, firmly affirmed its falsity.

In this same verse of al-Ahqaf there is another clear proof of its falsity: Allah explicitly stated that those who uttered that statement have had the word justified against them, and this is His saying: ﴿But the word has been justified from Me: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together."﴾ [As-Sajdah: 13]

It is well known that 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with both of them, embraced Islam and his Islam was good; he was among the best of the Muslims and the excellent Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The most that this noble verse implies is the use of alladhi to mean alladhina, which is common in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs, because the word alladhi is singular in form while its meaning is general to everything its relative clause (silah) includes. It is established in the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) that relative pronouns such as alladhi and allati and their derivatives are among the forms of generality, as he indicated in Maraqi al-Su'ud with his saying:

"The form of each, or the plural, and the derivatives of alladhi and allati have followed."

Among the instances in the Qur'an of alladhi being used to mean alladhina is this noble verse of Surah al-Ahqaf. And His saying in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿Their likeness is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], i.e., like the likeness of those who kindled, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, not seeing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], with the plural form in the three pronouns in bi-nurihim, wa-taraka-hum, and the waw in la yubsirun.

And His saying in al-Baqarah also: ﴿Like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264], i.e., like those who spend, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿They have no power over anything they have earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264].

• And His saying in az-Zumar: ﴿And the one who brings the truth and confirms it — those are the righteous﴾ [az-Zumar: 33].

• And His saying in at-Tawbah: ﴿And you engaged in vain talk as they engaged﴾ [at-Tawbah: 69].

i.e., like those who engaged, based on it being a relative pronoun and not a verbal noun (masdariyyah). A parallel from the speech of the Arabs is the saying of Ashhab ibn Rumaylah:

"Indeed those whose blood was spilled at Falj, they are the people, the entire people, O mother of Khalid."

And the saying of 'Udayl ibn al-Farkh al-'Ijli:

"I spent the night serving my brothers, those whose error is my error and whose right guidance is my right guidance."

And the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

"O Lord, may 'Abs not be blessed in anyone,
neither in one of them who stands nor one who sits,
except those who stood at the edges of the palm-fiber rope."

As for His saying in this noble verse: "Uff to you both" is an expression of annoyance. The one who says this is undutiful to his parents and does not heed the prohibition of Allah in His saying: ﴿If one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. His saying "Do you threaten me" (a'tidanni) is a verb, the present tense of wa'ada, and the deletion of its waw in the present tense is regular, as mentioned in al-Khulasah with his saying:

"From the imperative or present of kawa'ada, delete [the waw]; and in 'iddah that is regular."

The first nun is the nun of the raf' (nominative marker), and the second is the nun of protection (nun al-wiqayah), as is not hidden.

Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir in the narration of Ibn Dhakwan, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read this word as a'tidanni, with two kasra-marked light nuns and a sukun ya'.

Hisham, from Ibn 'Amir, read it with a shaddah-marked kasra nun and a sukun ya'.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read it with two kasra-marked light nuns and a fathah-marked ya', the hamzah being for denial (istinkar).

His saying "that I will be brought forth" means that I will be raised from my grave alive after death.

The verbal noun formed from an-and-its-clause is the second object of ta'iduannI, meaning: do you threaten me with my going forth from my grave alive after death? The situation is that the generations have passed, i.e., the earlier nations have perished, and none of them has come back to life or returned after dying.

"And they both" (wa-huma), i.e., his two parents, "call upon Allah for help" (yasta'ithan Allah), i.e., they ask Him to give them relief by guiding their son to the truth and to acknowledging the Resurrection. They say to their son: "Woe to you! Believe," i.e., in Allah and in the Resurrection after death.

What is meant by their saying "Woe to you" is urging him to faith. "Indeed the promise of Allah is true," i.e., His promise of resurrection after death is true without doubt. Then that undutiful son who denies the Resurrection says: "This is nothing but the myths of the former peoples," i.e., what you promise me of resurrection after death is nothing but the myths of the ancients.

Al-asatir is the plural of ustura. It was said it is the plural of istara, and what is meant by it is what the earlier people wrote down, i.e., things they recorded that have no reality.

His saying "Those" (ula'ika) refers to the undutiful deniers of the Resurrection mentioned in His saying: ﴿And the one who said to his parents, "Uff to you both"﴾ and so on.

His saying "upon whom the word has been justified" means the word of punishment has become binding upon them.

We have already mentioned the verses clarifying this in Surah Ya-Sin in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Certainly the word has been justified against most of them, so they do not believe﴾ [Ya-Sin: 7].

And what this noble verse indicates, that the deniers of the Resurrection have the word justified against them because of their disbelief, we have already mentioned the verses clarifying it in Surah al-Furqan in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blazing fire﴾ [al-Furqan: 11].

The Almighty said: ﴿And on the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire, [it will be said], "You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them. So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation, because you were arrogant in the earth without right and because you were defiantly disobedient."﴾

The meaning of this noble verse is that the disbelievers will be told, on the Day they are exposed to the Fire: ﴿You squandered your good things﴾.

As for "they are exposed to the Fire" (yuʿraḍūna ʿalā al-nār), some scholars said its meaning is that they will directly experience its heat, like the Arabs' saying, "He exposed them to the sword" when he killed them with it. This is a well-known meaning in Arabic speech.

Allah mentioned something similar to what is mentioned here in His saying: ﴿And on the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "Is this not the truth?"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 34]. This shows that the intended meaning of "exposure" is the direct experience of punishment, because of His saying: ﴿They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ [6]. Also His saying: ﴿And there surrounded the people of Pharaoh the worst of punishment: the Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ [Ghafir: 45–46], because it is the exposure of punishment.

Some scholars said that their exposure to the Fire means bringing them near to it and unveiling it for them so that they see it, as Allah said: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 53]. And He said: ﴿And Hell will be brought forth that Day﴾ [al-Fajr: 23].

Some scholars said there is inversion (qalb) in the sentence, and this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and others. They said the meaning is: "And on the Day the Fire is exposed to those who disbelieved." They said this is like the Arabs' saying, "I presented the she-camel to the watering trough," meaning "I presented the watering trough to the she-camel." They said this is supported by Allah's saying: ﴿And We will present Hell that Day to the disbelievers, in presentation﴾ [al-Kahf: 100].

The one who wrote this, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: This type of inversion mentioned in the verse, like inverting the subject to be the object and the object to be the subject and the like, has been disputed among the scholars of Arabic. The rhetoricians (ʿulamāʾ al-balāghah, the experts in eloquence) prohibited it except in comparison (tashbīh), so they permitted inverting the compared to be the comparer and the comparer to be the compared, on condition that this contains a subtle point and a fine secret, as is well known to them in the discussion of reversed comparison (al-tashbīh al-maqlūb).

Many scholars of Arabic permitted it.

What appears to us is that it is an Arabic style which the Arabs spoke in their language. However, what was heard from it is preserved and is not analogised upon. Among its examples in comparison is the words of the rajaz poet:

"A watering place whose surroundings are dusty, whose sky is like the colour of its earth."

That is: "as if its sky were the colour of its earth." And the words of another:

"Dawn appeared as if its brightness were the face of the caliph when he is praised."

Because the original intent is the comparison of the caliph's face to the brightness of dawn, but he inverted the comparison so as to give the impression that the branch is stronger than the root in the aspect of similarity.

They said: Among its examples in the Qur'an is: ﴿And We gave him of the treasures that its keys would burden a band of strong men﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], because it is the band of men who are burdened by the keys, meaning they rise with them with hardship and effort due to their abundance and weight. And His saying: ﴿So the news became obscure to them﴾ [al-Qasas: 66], meaning they were blind to it.

Among its examples in the speech of the Arabs is the words of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr:

"As if the return of her two forelegs, when she sweats, while she is wrapped in great rocks and mirages..."

Because the meaning of his words "talaffaʿa" is that she wore the wrap (lifāʿ), which is a blanket. Al-qawr means large rocks, and al-ʿasāqīl means mirages.

The speech is inverted, because it is the great rocks that are wrapped in mirages, not the reverse, as Labid clarified in his Muʿallaqah with his words:

"So in that time, when the shimmering things danced in the forenoon, and its mounds clothed themselves in the robes of mirage."

He explicitly stated that the mounds, which are rocks, clothed themselves, meaning wore, the robes of mirage.

The word "ardiyah" is the plural of "ridaʾ" (cloak). And this type of inversion, although some permitted it, it is not appropriate to apply it to the verse (p. 229), because it contradicts the apparent meaning, and there is no evidence requiring recourse to it.

The apparent meaning of the verse follows the eloquent Arabic style, as Abu Hayyan clarified in al-Bahr al-Muhit.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them﴾, Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʿAmir recited it as "a-adhhabtum" with two hamzas, and these two follow their respective principles in that.

Ibn Kathir softens the second hamza without inserting an alif between the two hamzas.

Hisham realises it and softens it with the inserted alif. Ibn Dhakwan realises it without insertion.

Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Hamzah and al-Kisaʾi recited it as "adhhabtum tayyibatikum" with one hamza, as a statement and not as a question.

Know that the scholars have much to say on this verse, saying that it indicates that one should practise asceticism and limit the enjoyment of foods, drinks, clothing and the like.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, used to do this out of fear that he would enter under the general application of those who will be told on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life﴾, to the end of the verse. The exegetes mention here many reports on this matter, and the conditions of the People of the Suffah (Ahl al-Suffah) and what they endured of severe hardship in living.

The one who wrote this, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The verified view, Allah willing, regarding the meaning of this verse is that it concerns the disbelievers, and not the believers who enjoy the pleasures which Allah has permitted for them; because He, the Exalted, did not permit them so that they would squander their good deeds through them.

We only say that this is the verified view because the Book and the authentic Sunnah both indicate it, and Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 59], to the end of the verse.

As for the verse being about the disbelievers, Allah has explicitly stated it in His saying: ﴿And on the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "You squandered your good things"﴾, to the end of the verse.

The Qur'an and the authentic Sunnah have indicated that if the disbeliever does a righteous deed conforming to the Sharia, sincere in it for Allah, such as one who is dutiful to his parents, keeps family ties, hosts the guest, relieves the distressed, and helps the oppressed, seeking thereby the face of Allah, he will be rewarded for his deed in this world only, with provision and well-being and the like, and he has no share in the Hereafter.

Among the verses indicating this is His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the worldly life and its adornment, We will fully repay them for their deeds therein, and they therein will not be deprived. Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire, and what they did therein is nullified, and worthless is what they used to do﴾ [Hud: 15–16]. And His saying: ﴿And whoever desires the harvest of this world, We will give him from it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20].

Allah has restricted this worldly reward mentioned in these verses by His will and His choice, in His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We desire﴾ ﴿Then We have made for him Hell, which he will enter, blamed and banished﴾ [al-Isra': 18].

It has been established in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, Allah does not wrong a believer a good deed; he is given for it in this world and is recompensed for it in the Hereafter. As for the disbeliever, he is fed for his good deeds which he did for Allah in this world, until when he reaches the Hereafter, he has no good deed for which he will be recompensed." This is the wording of Muslim in his Sahih.

And in another wording of his from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Indeed, when the disbeliever does a good deed, he is given a morsel for it in this world. As for the believer, Allah stores up his good deeds for him in the Hereafter, and gives him provision in this world as a consequence of his obedience." End of quotation.

This hadith established from the Prophet ﷺ contains an explicit statement that the disbeliever is recompensed for his good deeds in this world only, and that the believer is recompensed for his good deeds in both this world and the Hereafter together. By necessity, it is definitively determined, with no escape from it, that the one who squandered his good things in this world and enjoyed them is the disbeliever, because he is not recompensed for his good deeds except in this world only.

As for the believer, who is recompensed for his good deeds in both this world and the Hereafter together, he has not squandered his good things in this world, because his good deeds are stored up for him in the Hereafter, although Allah rewards him for them in this world, as Allah said: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ ﴿and will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 2–3]. So He made the way out of hardship for him and provided for him from where he does not expect, as reward in this world, and it does not diminish the reward of his piety in the Hereafter.

Verses similar to this are many and well known. In any case, Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, permitted His servants, through the tongue of His Prophet ﷺ, the good things in the worldly life, and permitted them to enjoy them, and yet made them exclusively theirs in the Hereafter, as Allah said: ﴿Say, "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?" Say, "They are for those who believed in the worldly life, purely [for them] on the Day of Resurrection"﴾ [al-A'raf: 32].

This Qur'anic text indicates that the believers' enjoyment of adornment and the good things of provision in the worldly life did not prevent them from being exclusively entitled to enjoying these on the Day of Resurrection, and it is explicit that they did not squander their good things in their worldly life.

Nor does it contradict this that whoever was suffering severe poverty in this world, like the People of the Suffah, will have an additional reward beyond that; because believers are rewarded for the calamities and hardships which befall them in this world, as is well known.

As for the texts indicating that the disbeliever is the one who squanders his good things in the worldly life, because he is recompensed in this world only, like the aforementioned verses, and the hadith of Anas mentioned in Muslim, we have already presented them clarified in Surat "Bani Isra'il," in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its striving while he is a believer, those are the ones whose striving will be appreciated﴾, and we mentioned there the chains of narration (asanid) of the mentioned hadith and its wordings.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, meaning the punishment of degradation, which is abasement and disgrace.

As for His saying: ﴿because you were arrogant in the earth without right and because you were defiantly disobedient﴾: the "bi" in "bi-mā kuntum" is causal (sababiyyah), and "mā" is verbal-masdariyyah, meaning: you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation because of your being arrogant in the earth, and your being defiantly disobedient.

What this noble verse indicates, that arrogance in the earth and defiant disobedience are among the causes of the punishment of humiliation, which is the punishment of the Fire, has come explained in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Is there not in Hell a residence for the arrogant?﴾ [al-Zumar: 60], and His saying: ﴿As for those who defied, their refuge is the Fire﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Sajdah: 20].

We have already presented the disastrous consequences resulting from arrogance in Surat "al-A'raf," in the discussion of His saying: ﴿It is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾, to the end of the verse [al-A'raf: 13].

(p. 232) As for His saying: ﴿without right﴾, although it is known that they are not arrogant in the earth except with an arrogance clothed in what is not right, like His saying: ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38], and it is known that it does not fly except with its two wings; and His saying: ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79], and it is known that they do not write it except with their own hands; and similar verses. This is an Arabic style in which the Qur'an was revealed.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 46, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention the brother of ʿĀd, when he warned his people in al-Aḥqāf.﴾

In this noble verse, He, may He be exalted, left the brother of ʿĀd unnamed and did not specify him. However, He specified in other verses that he was Hūd, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to ʿĀd We sent their brother Hūd﴾ in Surat al-Aʿrāf [al-Aʿrāf: 65], and Surat Hūd [Hūd: 50], and other passages.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That you worship none but Allah. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾

In this noble verse, He, may He be exalted, mentioned that the Prophet Hūd forbade his people to worship other than Allah, commanded them to worship Him alone, and warned them of the punishment of Allah if they persisted in their polytheism.

These two matters contained in this verse have been clarified in other verses.

As for the first of them, it is in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to ʿĀd We sent their brother Hūd. He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him﴾ in Surat al-Aʿrāf [al-Aʿrāf: 65], and Surat Hūd [Hūd: 50], and similar verses.

As for his fear for them of the great punishment, he mentioned it in al-Shuʿarāʾ, in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fear Him who has provided you with what you know. He provided you with livestock and children, and gardens and springs. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 132–135]. And that day is the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 46, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods? So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are of the truthful."﴾

And the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to turn us away from our gods﴾, i.e., to divert us from worshipping them to worshipping Allah alone.

This noble verse includes two matters: (p-233) The first: the denial by 'Ad of Hud, that he had come to them so that they would abandon the worship of idols and worship Allah alone.

The second: that they said to him: Bring us what you threaten us with of punishment, and hasten it for us, if you are truthful in what you say, out of their obstinacy and arrogance.

These two matters have been clarified in other places, such as His saying, may He be exalted, in "al-A'raf": ﴿They said, "Have you come to us that we should worship Allah alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are of the truthful."﴾ [al-A'raf: 70].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 46, verse 23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I convey to you that with which I have been sent﴾.

In this noble verse, He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, mentions that the Prophet of Allah, Hud, said to his people that he conveys to them that with which he was sent to them, because there is upon him nothing but conveyance (al-balagh). This meaning is mentioned in other places, such as His saying, may He be exalted, in "al-A'raf": ﴿He said, "O my people, there is no folly in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds. I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am to you a trustworthy adviser"﴾ [al-A'raf: 67-68]. And His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat "Hud": ﴿But if you turn away, then I have already conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you﴾, the verse [Hud: 57].

The Exalted said: ﴿Nay, it is that which you were hastening (to bring on): a wind wherein is a painful punishment.﴾

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in the surah "Fussilat" (Ha-Mim al-Sajdah), in the discussion of the Exalted's words: ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind during days of misfortune.﴾ [Fussilat: 16].

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَلَقَدْ مَكَّنّاهم فِيما إنَّ مَكَّنّاكم فِيهِ﴾ .

[Commentary on the Qur'anic verse: "And We had certainly established them in that wherein We have not established you."]

لَفْظَةُ إنْ في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ الكَرِيمَةِ فِيها لِلْمُفَسِّرِينَ ثَلاثَةُ أوْجُهٍ، يَدُلُّ اسْتِقْراءُ القُرْآنِ عَلى أنَّ واحِدًا مِنها هو الحَقُّ، دُونَ الِاثْنَيْنِ الآخَرَيْنِ.

The word إنْ (in) in this noble verse has three interpretations among the exegetes. The inductive study of the Qur'an indicates that one of them is the truth, to the exclusion of the other two.

قالَ بَعْضُ العُلَماءِ: إنْ شَرْطِيَّةٌ، وجَزاءُ الشَّرْطِ مَحْذُوفٌ، والتَّقْدِيرُ إنْ مَكَّنّاكم فِيهِ طَغَيْتُمْ وبَغَيْتُمْ.

Some scholars said: إنْ is conditional (shartiyyah), and the response of the condition is omitted. The implied meaning is: "If We had established you in it, you would have transgressed and oppressed."

وَقالَ بَعْضُهم: إنْ زائِدَةٌ بَعْدَ ما المَوْصُولَةِ حَمْلًا لِـ ما المَوْصُولَةِ عَلى ما النّافِيَةِ؛ لِأنَّ ما النّافِيَةَ تُزادُ بَعْدَها لَفْظَةُ إنْ كَما هو مَعْلُومٌ.

Others said: إنْ is superfluous (zā'idah) after the relative ما (mawṣūlah), by analogy of the relative ما to the negating ما (nāfiyah), since after the negating ما the word إنْ is commonly added, as is well known.

(p-٢٣٤)كَقَوْلِ قُتَيْلَةَ بِنْتِ الحارِثِ أوِ النَّضْرِ العَبْدَرِيَّةِ:

As in the verse of Qutaylah bint al-Harith, or al-Nadr al-Abdariyyah:

؎أبْلِغْ بِها مَيْتًا بِأنَّ تَحِيَّةً ما إنْ نَزِلَّ بِها النَّجائِبَ تُخْفِقُوا

"Convey through her to one dead that a greeting—when the swift camels alight with it, they would not stir up dust..."

وَقَوْلِ دُرَيْدِ بْنِ الصِّمَّةِ في الخَنْساءِ:

And the verse of Durayd ibn al-Simmah concerning al-Khansa:

؎ما إنْ رَأيْتُ ولا سَمِعْتُ بِهِ ∗∗∗ كاليَوْمِ طالِي أيَنُقٍ جُرْبِ

"I have neither seen nor heard of anything like today's [driver] of mangy she-camels."

فَـ (إنْ) زائِدَةٌ بَعْدَ (ما) النّافِيَةِ في البَيْتَيْنِ، وهو كَثِيرٌ، وقَدْ حَمَلُوا عَلى ذَلِكَ (ما) المَوْصُولَةَ، فَقالُوا: تُزادُ بَعْدَها (إنْ) كَآيَةِ ”الأحْقافِ“ هَذِهِ. وأنْشَدَ لِذَلِكَ الأخْفَشُ: يُرَجِّي المَرْءُ ما إنْ لا يَراهُ وتَعْرِضُ دُونَ أدْناهُ الخُطُوبُ

In both verses, (إنْ) is superfluous after the negating (ما), which is common. They analogized the relative (ما) to it and said that (إنْ) is added after it, as in this verse of al-Ahqaf. al-Akhfash cited for this: "A man hopes for what he does not see, while calamities stand between him and its nearest."

أيْ يُرْجِّي المَرْءُ الشَّيْءَ الَّذِي لا يَراهُ، وإنْ زائِدَةٌ، وهَذانِ هُما الوَجْهانِ اللَّذانِ لا تَظْهَرُ صِحَّةُ واحِدٍ مِنهُما.

That is: a man hopes for the thing he does not see, and إنْ is superfluous. These are the two interpretations whose soundness is not evident.

لِأنَّ الأوَّلَ مِنهُما فِيهِ حَذْفٌ وتَقْدِيرٌ.

Because the first of them involves omission and implied content.

والثّانِي مِنهُما فِيهِ زِيادَةُ كَلِمَةٍ.

And the second involves the addition of a word.

وَكُلُّ ذَلِكَ لا يُصارُ إلَيْهِ إلّا بِدَلِيلٍ يَجِبُ الرُّجُوعُ إلَيْهِ.

None of this is resorted to except by a proof to which one must return.

أمّا الوَجْهُ الثّالِثُ الَّذِي هو الصَّوابُ - إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ - فَهو أنَّ لَفْظَةَ (إنْ) نافِيَةٌ بَعْدَ (ما) المَوْصُولَةِ، أيْ ولَقَدْ مَكَّنّاهم في الَّذِي ما مَكَّنّاكم فِيهِ مِنَ القُوَّةِ في الأجْسامِ، وكَثْرَةِ الأمْوالِ والأوْلادِ والعَدَدِ.

As for the third interpretation, which is the correct one, God willing, it is that the word (إنْ) is negating (nāfiyah) after the relative (ما): that is, "And We had certainly established them in that which We had not established you in, of strength of bodies, abundance of wealth, children, and number."

وَإنَّما قُلْنا: إنَّ القُرْآنَ يَشْهَدُ لِهَذا القَوْلِ لِكَثْرَةِ الآياتِ الدّالَّةِ عَلَيْهِ، فَإنَّ اللَّهَ - جَلَّ وعَلا - في آياتٍ كَثِيرَةٍ مِن كِتابِهِ يُهَدِّدُ كُفّارَ مَكَّةَ بِأنَّ الأُمَمَ الماضِيَةَ كانَتْ أشَدَّ مِنهم بَطْشًا وقُوَّةً، وأكْثَرَ مِنهم عَدَدًا وأمْوالًا وأوْلادًا، فَلَمّا كَذَّبُوا الرُّسُلَ أهْلَكَهُمُ اللَّهُ لِيَخافُوا مِن تَكْذِيبِ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ أنْ يُهْلِكَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِسَبَبِهِ، كَما أهْلَكَ الأُمَمَ الَّتِي هي أقْوى مِنهم، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعالى في ”المُؤْمِنِ“: ﴿أفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا في الأرْضِ فَيَنْظُرُوا كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ كانُوا أكْثَرَ مِنهم وأشَدَّ قُوَّةً وآثارًا في الأرْضِ فَما أغْنى عَنْهم ما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ [غافر: ٨٢] .

We said that the Qur'an bears witness to this view because of the abundance of verses indicating it. God, Mighty and Majestic, in many verses of His Book threatens the disbelievers of Makkah that the earlier nations were stronger than them in might and power, and greater than them in number, wealth and children. When they denied the messengers, God destroyed them, so that the people (of Makkah) would fear that God might destroy them for their denial of the Prophet ﷺ, just as He destroyed the nations that were stronger than them. As in His saying in "al-Mu'min": "Have they not travelled in the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in number and stronger in might and in traces left upon the earth, yet what they used to earn did not avail them." [Ghafir: 82]

وَقَوْلُهُ فِيها أيْضًا: ﴿أوَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا في الأرْضِ فَيَنْظُرُوا كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ كانُوا مِن قَبْلِهِمْ كانُوا هم أشَدَّ مِنهم قُوَّةً وآثارًا في الأرْضِ فَأخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ الآيَةَ [غافر: ٢١] .

And His saying in the same surah: "Have they not travelled in the earth and seen how was the end of those who were before them? They were stronger than them in might and in traces upon the earth, so God seized them for their sins..." [Ghafir: 21]

(p-٢٣٥)وَقَوْلُهُ تَعالى في ”الرُّومِ“: ﴿أوَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا في الأرْضِ فَيَنْظُرُوا كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ كانُوا أشَدَّ مِنهم قُوَّةً وأثارُوا الأرْضَ وعَمَرُوها أكْثَرَ مِمّا عَمَرُوها﴾ الآيَةَ [الروم: ٩] .

And His saying in "al-Rum": "Have they not travelled in the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? They were stronger than them in might, and they ploughed the earth and built it up more than they have built it up..." [al-Rum: 9]

وَقَدْ قَدَّمْنا الآياتِ المُوَضِّحَةَ لِهَذا في سُورَةِ ”الزُّخْرُفِ“ في الكَلامِ عَلى قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿فَأهْلَكْنا أشَدَّ مِنهم بَطْشًا ومَضى مَثَلُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ [الزخرف: ١٠] .

We have already presented the verses clarifying this in surah "al-Zukhruf," in discussing His saying: "So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might, and the example of the former peoples has passed." [al-Zukhruf: 8]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 46, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why then did those whom they had taken as gods besides Allah, as a means of nearness, not help them? Rather, they vanished from them. That was their falsehood and what they used to fabricate.﴾

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah al-Jathiyah, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Neither their earnings nor those they took as protectors besides Allah will avail them anything, and for them is a great punishment﴾ [the verse, 10].

**The words of Allah, the Exalted:** ﴿When We turned towards you a group of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an. When they attended it, they said, "Be silent." When it was finished, they returned to their people as warners.﴾ ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path."﴾

Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in this noble verse of Surah "al-Ahqaf" that He turned to the Prophet (ﷺ) ﴿a group of the jinn﴾. The *nafar* (group) is fewer than ten. ﴿They were listening to the Qur'an﴾, and when they attended it, some of them said to others: "*Anṣitū*," meaning "be silent and listen." When it was finished, meaning when the Prophet (ﷺ) finished his recitation, they ﴿returned﴾, meaning they went back to their people among the jinn, ﴿as warners﴾, meaning they warned them of the punishment of Allah if they did not believe in Allah and respond to His caller, Muhammad (ﷺ). They informed their people that this Book they had heard being recited, the one sent down after Moses, ﴿guides to the truth﴾, which is the opposite of falsehood, ﴿and to a straight path﴾, meaning there is no crookedness in it.

The Great Qur'an shows that the listening of these jinn, and what they said about the Qur'an, all of it, took place without the Prophet (ﷺ) knowing about it until Allah revealed that to him. Allah said about this same story, explaining it in detail and describing the statements the jinn made after they had listened to the Great Qur'an: ﴿Say, "It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened, and they said, 'We have heard a wondrous Qur'an, which guides to right conduct, so we believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.'"﴾ [al-Infitar: 1-2], and so on to the end of the verses.

[p. 236] His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of God and believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾.

The explicit meaning (mantuq) of this verse is that whoever responds to the caller of God, Muhammad (ﷺ), and believes in him and in what he brought of the truth, God will forgive his sins and protect him from the painful punishment. Its implicit meaning (mafhum), namely the implication of its opposite (mafhum al-mukhalafa, the contrary implication, known as dalalat al-khitab, "indication of the discourse"), is that whoever does not respond to the caller of God from among the jinn, and does not believe in him, will not be forgiven and will not be protected from the painful punishment; rather, He will punish him and cause him to enter the Fire. This implication is stated explicitly and clarified in other verses, such as:

- His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and humans all together"﴾ [Hud 11:119].
- His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and humans all together"﴾ [as-Sajdah 32:13].
- His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He will say: "Enter into the Fire among nations of jinn and humans who passed away before you"﴾ [al-A'raf 7:38].
- His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators, and the hosts of Iblis, all together﴾ [ash-Shu'ara 26:94–95].

And other verses besides these.

As for the entry of the believing jinn who responded to the caller of God into Paradise, this noble verse does not address it either by affirmation or by negation. Another verse does indicate that believing jinn enter Paradise, namely His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat ar-Rahman: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [ar-Rahman 55:46–47]. From this you know that what some scholars have held, saying that this verse implies that believing jinn do not enter Paradise, and that the reward of their faith and their response to the caller of God is only forgiveness and protection from the painful punishment, as the literal text of the verse states, is entirely contrary to the careful verification (tahqiq).

We have clarified this in our book Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), in discussing this verse from Surat al-Ahqaf. There we said the following, quoting it verbatim: "This verse implies from its apparent meaning that the reward of the obedient among the jinn is the forgiveness of their sins and protection from the painful punishment, not their entry into Paradise."

A group of scholars, among them the Imam Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, have adhered to the apparent meaning of this verse, saying that obedient believing jinn do not enter Paradise. Yet another verse indicates that their believers are in Paradise, namely His saying: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾, because He explained that it includes both jinn and humans in His saying: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾.

[p. 237] This is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾ [ar-Rahman 55:56]. It indicates that there are jinn in Paradise who have intercourse with women as humans do.

The answer to this is that the verse of al-Ahqaf explicitly mentions forgiveness and protection from the punishment, and does not address entry into Paradise either by negation or affirmation. The verse of ar-Rahman explicitly mentions their entry into Paradise, because He said in it: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾.

It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that relative pronouns (al-mawsulat) are among the forms of generality (sigha al-'umum). Thus His saying ﴿for whoever fears﴾ encompasses every one who fears the standing before his Lord. Then He explicitly stated that this includes both jinn and humans together, in His saying: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾.

So He made clear that the promise of the two gardens for whoever fears the standing before his Lord is among His favours, that is, His blessings upon humans and jinn. There is therefore no contradiction between the two verses, because each one clarifies what the other did not address.

Even if we grant that His saying ﴿He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾ implies that they do not enter Paradise, that is only by implication (mafhum), whereas His saying ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ indicates their entry into Paradise by the general explicit meaning (mantuq). The explicit meaning takes precedence over the implicit meaning, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence.

There is no doubt that if we want to verify this claimed implication, we find that it does not exist at all. This is because there is consensus that the division of implications is twofold: either it is an implication of concordance (mafhum al-muwafaqa) or an implication of contrariety (mafhum al-mukhalafa), and there is no third category.

This claimed implication does not fall under any category of the two types. As for its not falling under the implication of concordance in either of its two forms, that is clear. As for its not falling under any type of the implication of contrariety, that is because its not falling under the implication of restriction (hasr), the implication of limit (ghaya), the implication of number ('adad), the implication of attribute (sifa), or the implication of circumstance (zarf) is clear.

Therefore, among the types of the implication of contrariety, there remains only the implication of condition (mafhum al-shart) or the implication of the title (mafhum al-laqab) that could be suspected as including it. It does not fall under either of them, so it becomes clear that it does not fall under them at all.

As for the reason it might be suspected of falling under the implication of condition: His saying ﴿He will forgive you some of your sins﴾ [p. 238] is a present-tense verb in the jussive mood (majzum), because it is the response (jawab) of an imperative.

The majority of Arabic grammarians hold that when the verb is like this, it is in the jussive mood because of an implied conditional particle (shart muqaddar), not because of the preceding clause, as some have claimed.

According to the correct view, which is the position of the majority, the meaning is: "Respond to the caller of God and believe in him; if you do that, He will forgive you." Thus the implication of this implied condition may be suspected in the verse.

The answer to this is that the implication of the condition, according to the one who holds it, applies only to the protasis (fi'l al-shart), not to its apodosis (jaza'). It is applied here to the protasis in the usual way. So the implication of "if you respond to the caller of God and believe in him, He will forgive you" is that if they do not respond to the caller of God and do not believe in him, He will not forgive them. And this is indeed the case.

As for the apodosis of the condition, it has no implication, because one condition may have many consequences, so some of them are mentioned as the apodosis, and this does not indicate the negation of the others.

As when you say to a person, for example: "If you steal, you must pay for what you stole." This statement is true, and it does not indicate the negation of other consequences, such as amputation, because the amputation of the hand is also a consequence of theft, as is the payment.

Likewise, forgiveness, protection from punishment, and entry into Paradise are all consequences of responding to the caller of God and believing in him. The verse mentions some of them and is silent about others, and then another passage clarifies them. There is no difficulty in this.

As for the reason it might be suspected of falling under the implication of the title, this is because the title (laqab), in the terminology of the jurists of usul, is that without which the structure of Arabic speech cannot be formed, namely the subject of the sentence (musnad ilayh), whether it is a title, a kunya (teknonym), a proper name, a generic noun, or otherwise.

We have clarified the title in full detail in our discussion of Surat al-Ma'idah.

The answer to the claim that it does not fall under the implication of the title is that forgiveness and protection from the punishment, which are claimed to be titles for the class of their verbal nouns, and that singling them out in mention indicates the negation of anything other than them in the verse, are predicates (sanad), not subjects (musnad ilayhi), for them. The proof is that the verbal noun in them is latent in the verb, and it is agreed that it is not predicated of the verb (ila al-fi'l) unless its bare form is mentioned by way of quotation (hikaya).

[p. 239] The implication of the title, according to the one who holds it, applies only when the title is the subject. This is because singling it out in mention, according to the one who holds it, indicates that the ruling is restricted to it and not to anything else. Otherwise, singling it out in mention would have no purpose, as they gave as a reason for the implication of the attribute.

It is answered on behalf of the majority: the title is mentioned so that the ruling can be attached to it, not to restrict the ruling to it, since predication is not possible without a subject.

What clarifies this is that the implication of the attribute, on which the title is modelled according to the one who holds it, applies only to the subject, not to the predicate. This is because the subject is the thing whose individual members and their attributes are taken into account, so some of them are intended in mention rather than others, and thus the ruling is restricted to what is mentioned.

As for the predicate, nothing of its individuals or attributes is taken into account at all. Rather, only the bare quiddity (mahiyya), which is the mental reality (haqiqa dhihniyya), is taken into account.

For example, if you judge that man is an animal, the subject, which is man in this example, is intended with all its individuals, because each one of them is an animal. By contrast, the predicate, which is animal in this example, is intended only with its absolute quiddity and mental reality, without regard to individuals. For if its individuals were taken into account, the judgment about man would entail that he is another individual of animals, like a carpet, for example.

The judgment of a predicate of one category upon a subject of a different category is invalid when it is affirmative, by the agreement of rational people.

The general body of theorists hold that when the subject of a proposition is not natural (ghayr tabi'iyya), the individuals to which its heading applies are taken into account: if it is external (kharijiyya), by its existence in the external world; if it is true (haqiqiyya), by its mental existence.

As for the predicate as such, individuals are never taken into account at all. Only the absolute quiddity is taken into account.

Even if we grant, for the sake of argument, that a verse such as this falls under the implication of the title, the majority of scholars hold that the implication of the title has no weight, and that to consider it may even amount to unbelief. For example, if someone considered the implication of the title in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of God﴾ [al-Fath 48:29], and said: "It is understood from the implication of his title that anyone other than Muhammad (ﷺ) was not a messenger of God," this would be unbelief by the consensus of the Muslims.

The truth is that considering the implication of the title has no evidence for it, whether from the Shari'ah, from language, or from reason, whether the term is a generic noun, a proper noun, a collective noun, or otherwise.

[p. 240] Your saying, "Zayd came," does not imply that 'Amr did not come. Your saying, "I saw a lion," does not imply that you did not see anything other than a lion.

The view that distinguishes between a generic noun, which is taken into account, and a proper noun, which is not, is not evident.

Therefore, no weight is given to the view of as-Sayrafi, Abu Bakr ad-Daqqaq, and others among the Shafi'is, nor to the view of Ibn Khuwayz Mandad and Ibn al-Qassar among the Malikis, nor to the view of some Hanbalis who take the implication of the title into account. This is because there is no evidence for its consideration even according to the one who holds it, except that he says: "If the title were not restricted to the ruling, singling it out in mention would have no purpose," as he gave as a reason for the implication of the attribute. The majority, however, say: "The title is mentioned so that the predicate can be attached to it." This is clear and has no difficulty.

The author of Maraqi as-Su'ud has alluded to the definition of the title in the technical terminology of usul and to the fact that it is the weakest of the implications, in his verse:

"The weakest of them is the title, without which the structure of Arabic speech cannot be formed."

The essence of the jurisprudence of this question is as follows. The jinn are obligated through the words of our Prophet (ﷺ), by the indication of the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Muslims. Their disbelievers are in the Fire by the consensus of the Muslims, and this is the explicit statement of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and humans all together﴾ [Hud 11:119].

Also His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators, and the hosts of Iblis, all together﴾ [ash-Shu'ara 26:94–95].

Also His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He will say: "Enter into the Fire among nations of jinn and humans who passed away before you"﴾ [al-A'raf 7:38].

And other verses besides these.

As for their believers, there is disagreement about whether they enter Paradise, and the source of the disagreement is the difference in understanding the two verses mentioned.

The apparent view is that they enter Paradise, as we have explained, and God knows best. End of quotation, in his own words.

The author said in Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of God and believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾.

This verse implies from its apparent meaning that the reward of the obedient among the jinn is the forgiveness of their sins and protection from the painful punishment, not their entry into Paradise.

(p-391) Some scholars, among them the Imam Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, relied on the apparent meaning of this verse and said that believing jinn who obey do not enter Paradise. Yet another verse indicates that their believers are in Paradise, namely His words, exalted is He: "But for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens" (Ar-Rahman 55:46). He, exalted is He, made clear that it includes both jinn and humans by His words: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" (Ar-Rahman 55:47). This is further supported by His words, exalted is He: "Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them" (Ar-Rahman 55:56), since it points to the presence in Paradise of jinn who have intercourse with women, as humans do.

The answer to this is that the verse of "al-Ahqaf" explicitly mentions forgiveness and protection from punishment, and does not address entry into Paradise either by negation or affirmation. The verse of "ar-Rahman" explicitly mentions their entry into Paradise, since He, exalted is He, said in it: "But for whoever fears the standing before his Lord."

It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that relative pronouns (al-mawsulat) are among the forms of generality (sigha al-'umum). So His saying "for whoever fears" encompasses every one who fears the standing before his Lord. Then He stated explicitly that this includes both jinn and humans together, by His saying: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" Thus He made clear that the promise of the two gardens to whoever fears the standing before his Lord is among His favours (al-ala'), that is, His blessings upon humans and jinn. There is therefore no contradiction between the two verses, because each one clarifies what the other did not address. Even if we grant that His saying: "He will forgive you of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment" implies that they do not enter Paradise, it implies this only through implication (al-mafhum).

As for His saying, "But for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens" and "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?", they indicate their entry into Paradise through the generality of the stated meaning (al-manṭūq). The stated meaning takes precedence over the implied meaning, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence.

It should not be overlooked that if we investigate the implied meaning claimed here, we find that it has no basis at all, because there is consensus that the implied meaning is divided into two: either it is an implied meaning of agreement (mafhum al-muwafaqa) or of disagreement (mafhum al-mukhalafa), with no third category. This claimed implied meaning falls under neither of the two categories. That it does not fall under the implied meaning of agreement in either of its two kinds is clear. As for it not falling under any type of the implied meaning of disagreement, this is because its non-inclusion in the implied meaning of restriction (al-hasr), of cause ('illa), of limit (al-gháya), of number ('adad), of attribute (sifa), or of circumstance (al-zarf) is clear.

Therefore, among the types of the implied meaning of disagreement, there remains only one that could be thought to include it, namely the implied meaning of condition (mafhum al-shart) or of title (mafhum al-laqab). It is not included in either of these, and so its non-inclusion is shown to be absolute.

As for the reason it might be thought to fall under the implied meaning of condition: His saying "He will forgive you of your sins" is a present-tense verb (fi'l mudari') in the jussive mood (majzum) because it is the response (jaza') to a command (talab). The majority of Arabic scholars hold that when a verb is in this position, it is jussive by virtue of an implied condition (shart muqaddar), not by virtue of the clause before it, as some have claimed.

According to the correct view, which is the position of the majority, the meaning is: "Respond to the caller of God and believe in him; if you do that, He will forgive you." Thus, the implied condition may be thought to be present in the verse.

The answer to this is that the implied meaning of the condition, according to those who hold it, is only in the protasis (fi'l al-shart) and not in its apodosis (jaza'). It is considered here in the protasis according to its usual practice. So the implied meaning of "If you respond to the caller of God and believe in him, He will forgive you" is that if they do not respond to the caller of God and do not believe in him, He will not forgive them, and this is indeed the case. As for the apodosis of the condition, it has no implied meaning, because one condition may have many consequences, so some of them are mentioned as its apodosis, and this does not indicate the negation of the others. For example, if you say to a person: "If you steal, the compensation for what you stole will become obligatory for you," this statement is true, and it does not indicate the negation of anything other than compensation, such as amputation (al-qat'), because cutting off the hand is also a consequence of theft, just as compensation is. Likewise, forgiveness and protection from punishment, and entry into Paradise, are all consequences of responding to the caller of God and believing in him. So the verse mentions some of them and is silent about others, and then He clarified them in another place. There is no difficulty in this.

As for the reason it might be thought to fall under the implied meaning of title (mafhum al-laqab): the title, in the terminology of the jurists of principles, is what the Arabic sentence cannot be formed without, when it is the subject (al-musnad ilayhi), whether it is a proper name (laqab), a kunya, a noun, a generic noun (ism jins), or something else. We have explained the title thoroughly in the commentary on "al-Ma'ida."

The answer to the claim that it does not fall under the implied meaning of title is that forgiveness and protection from punishment, which are claimed to be titles for the genus of their verbal nouns, are, by hypothesis, predicates (musnad), not subjects (musnad ilayhi). The proof is that the verbal noun is implicit in the verb, and it is agreed that a verb is not predicated of a verb unless its bare wording is cited as a quotation.

The implied meaning of title, according to those who hold it, applies only when the title is the subject, because specifying it by mention, according to those who hold it, indicates that the ruling is restricted to it and not to anything else. Otherwise, there would be no benefit in specifying it by mention, just as they gave this as the reason for the implied meaning of attribute.

The majority have answered that the title is mentioned so that a ruling can be made about it, not so that the ruling is restricted to it, since a predication cannot happen without a subject. What clarifies this is that the implied meaning of attribute, on which the title is modelled by those who hold it, applies to the subject and not to the predicate, because the subject is the one whose individuals and their attributes are considered, so some of them are mentioned and not others, and the ruling is therefore restricted to what is mentioned.

As for the predicate, nothing of individuals or attributes is considered in it at all; only the bare quiddity (al-mahiyya), which is the mental reality, is considered.

So if you judge, for example, that "man is an animal," then the subject here, which is "man," is intended to include all its individuals, because each individual of it is an animal. By contrast, the predicate here, which is "animal," is intended only as the absolute quiddity and mental reality of the thing, without considering the individuals. For if its individuals were considered, the judgement about man would entail that he is another individual of animals, like a horse, for example.

A judgement of something opposite about something opposite is invalid, when it is affirmative, by the agreement of rational people and of the general body of theorists. Furthermore, when the subject of a proposition is not a natural one, what is considered in it is what its title applies to in terms of individuals, according to the external existence if it is an external proposition, or the mental existence if it is a real proposition.

As for the predicate considered in itself, individuals are not considered in it at all, only its absolute quiddity.

Even if we grant, for the sake of argument, that a verse like this falls under the implied meaning of title, the majority of scholars hold that the implied meaning of title has no weight, and that considering it may even be disbelief. An example is if someone considered the implied meaning of the title in His saying, exalted is He: "Muhammad is the Messenger of God" (Al-Fath 48:29), and said: "From the implied meaning of his title, it follows that anyone other than Muhammad is imagined and was not a Messenger of God." This is disbelief by the consensus of Muslims.

Therefore, the verified position is that considering the implied meaning of title has no evidence for it, either from the Shari'a, or from the Arabic language, or from reason, whether it is a generic noun, a proper noun, a collective noun, or something else.

Your saying "Zayd came" does not imply that 'Amr did not come. And your saying "I saw a lion" does not imply that you did not see anything other than a lion.

The view that distinguishes between a generic noun, which is considered, and a proper noun, which is not considered, does not hold. There is no weight to the view of al-Sayrafi, Abu Bakr al-Daqqaq and others among the Shafi'is, nor to the view of Ibn Khuwayz Mandad and Ibn al-Qassar among the Malikis, nor to the view of some Hanbalis who considered the implied meaning of title. For there is no evidence for its consideration according to those who hold it, except that he says: "If the title were not restricted to the ruling, there would be no benefit in specifying it by mention," just as he gave this as the reason for the implied meaning of attribute.

For the majority say: the title is mentioned so that a predication can be made about it. This is clear and has no difficulty.

The author of Maraqi al-Su'ud pointed to the definition of title in the technical terminology of the principles, and that it is the weakest of the implied meanings, in his words:

"The weakest of them is the title, which is that without which the Arabic sentence cannot be formed."

The summary of the legal point is that the jinn are morally responsible (mukallafun) through the words of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), by the indication of the Book, the Sunna, and the consensus of the Muslims. Their disbelievers are in the Fire by the consensus of the Muslims, and this is the explicit meaning of His saying, exalted is He: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together." And His saying, exalted is He: "So they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators. And the soldiers of Iblis, all together" (Ash-Shu'ara 26:94–95). And His saying, exalted is He: "He will say: Enter into the Fire among nations that have passed away before you of jinn and men" (Al-A'raf 7:38), and other verses besides these.

As for their believers, there is disagreement about whether they enter Paradise. The source of the disagreement is the difference in understanding the two verses mentioned. The apparent position is that they enter Paradise, as we have explained. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 46, verse 33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and did not tire in their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, indeed He is over all things competent.﴾

We have already mentioned the verses that clarify this verse, and that they are among the verses that indicate the resurrection (al-Ba'th), in (p-241) "al-Baqarah," "al-Nahl," "al-Jathiyah," and other places, and we have referred to that many times. The letter "bi" (ba') in His saying "bi-qadir" (able) is justified by the fact that the negation extends to "anna" (that) and what follows it, so it has the meaning of "Is not Allah able?"

What clarifies this is His saying afterward: "Yes" (bala), affirming His power over the resurrection and other things.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 46, verse 35:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So be patient, as the messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-azm) were patient﴾. The scholars differed greatly regarding the meaning of "those of firm resolve among the messengers" in this noble verse.

The most well-known of the opinions on this is that they are five, and they are the ones we previously mentioned in "al-Ahzab" and "al-Shura": Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them.

According to this opinion, the messengers whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to be patient as they were patient are four, so he ﷺ becomes the fifth of them.

Know that the view that the meaning of "those of firm resolve" is all the messengers, peace be upon them, and that the particle "min" in His words "min al-rusul" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), appears to be contrary to verification (al-tahqiq), as some Qur'anic verses indicate, such as His words: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ [al-Qalam: 48]. In this verse of "al-Qalam," Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded His Prophet to be patient and forbade him to be like Yunus, for he was the companion of the fish. And His words: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115]. The verse of "al-Qalam" and the verse of "Ta-Ha" that are both mentioned indicate that those of firm resolve among the messengers, whom the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to be patient as they were patient, are not all the messengers. And Allah knows best.

* *

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And do not hasten on their behalf﴾.

In this noble verse Allah forbade His Prophet ﷺ from seeking to hasten punishment upon his people, i.e., from praying to Allah against them for its hastening. The object of (tasta'jil, "hasten") is omitted, its estimated form being "the punishment," as al-Qurtubi said, and this is the apparent meaning.

What this noble verse includes of prohibition against seeking the hastening of punishment for them has been clarified in other verses, such as His words: ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11]. And His words: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them respite gradually﴾ [al-Tariq: 17].

Indeed His words: ﴿and give them respite a little﴾, and His words: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them respite gradually﴾, clarify the meaning of His words: ﴿and do not hasten on their behalf﴾.

What is meant by the verses is the prohibition for him ﷺ against seeking the hastening of punishment for them, because they will certainly be punished when the appointed period of respite ends, as His words clarify: ﴿So do not be hasty against them; We are only counting for them a count﴾ [Maryam: 84]. And His words: ﴿We provide them enjoyment for a little; then We will force them to a severe punishment﴾ [Luqman: 24]. And His words: ﴿He said, "As for one who disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little; then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126]. And His words: ﴿Let not your being deceived by the movement of those who disbelieve throughout the land﴾ ﴿a brief enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196-197]. And His words: ﴿Say, "Indeed, those who invent falsehood about Allah will not succeed"﴾ ﴿A enjoyment in this world; then to Us is their return; then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾ [Yunus: 69-70]. And other verses besides these.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿As if they, on the day they see what they are promised, had not remained but an hour of a day﴾.

We have already presented the verses clarifying this in surah "Yunus," in the discussion of His words: ﴿And the day He gathers them, as if they had not remained but an hour of the day, recognizing one another﴾ [Yunus: 45]. And in surah "Qad Aflaha al-Mu'minun," in the discussion of His words: ﴿They said, "We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who count"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 113].

And we explained, in the discussion of the verse ﴿Qad aflaha al-mu'minun﴾, the way of removing a well-known difficulty in the mentioned verses.

* *

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Balagh﴾.

The verification, if Allah wills, is that the more correct of the two opinions regarding His words "balagh" is that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being: "This is a balagh (message)," i.e., this Qur'an is a message (balagh) from Allah to His creation.

What supports this is His words in surah "Ibrahim": ﴿This is a message (balagh) for mankind, and that they may be warned by it﴾ [Ibrahim: 52]. And His words in "al-Anbiya": ﴿Indeed in this is a message (balagh) for a people who worship﴾ [al-Anbiya: 106]. And the best thing by which the Qur'an is interpreted is the Qur'an.

"Balagh" is a verbal noun meaning tabligh (conveying), and it is known by inductive study of the Arabic language that the pattern fi'al often comes in the meaning of tafil (the intensive form), as in ballaghahu balaghan, i.e., tablighan (he conveyed it to him), kallamahu kalaman, i.e., takliman (he spoke to him), tallaqaha talaqan, sarrahaha sarahan, and bayyanahu bayanan.

All of these are in the meaning of tafil, because fa''ala, with a doubled middle radical that is neither weak in its final letter nor hamzated, has as its verbal noun the pattern taf'il by analogy.

What comes from it contrary to this is preserved and not analogized upon, as is known in its proper place.

As for the view that the meaning is: "and that staying is a balagh," it is contrary to the apparent meaning, as you see. And Allah knows best.
